stages.title: Intermediate vocabulary
stages.hook: What is the difference between "big", "huge" and "enormous"? Words have shades of meaning.
explain: Intermediate vocabulary means more precise words. Synonyms have similar meanings but differ in strength or tone: big, large, huge, enormous. Antonyms are opposites: increase and decrease.

Word families help you grow your vocabulary. From the root "act" we get action, active, actor and actively. Prefixes such as un- and re- and suffixes such as -ful and -less change the meaning or the part of speech.
stages.mnemonic: One root, many branches: a word is a tree.
items: to find out about something new
a person who helps in a hospital
sentences: She felt hopeful about the exam.

gq.q: What does the prefix "un-" usually do?
o: Gives the opposite, as in unhappy
Makes a word plural, as in unhappies
gq.why: Un- often means not, as in unhappy or unkind.

gq.q: Which word means the same as "tiny"?
gq.why: Tiny and minute (my-NEWT) both mean very small.

panel.q: Which suffix turns the noun "care" into an adjective meaning "without care"?
panel.why: Careless means without care; careful means full of care.

panel.q: Why is "thin" a better choice than "skinny" in a formal description?
o: Skinny can sound negative; thin is neutral
They are different parts of speech
Skinny is always rude in every context
Thin is too informal and skinny is more formal
panel.why: Synonyms carry different connotations, so tone matters.

panel.q: How can word families help you learn vocabulary?
panel.model: If you know the root, you can guess related words made with prefixes and suffixes, so one word gives you several.
panel.why: Word formation multiplies vocabulary.

teach.topic: Growing your vocabulary with word families
teach.model: Many words come from one root. Add a prefix or suffix and you get a new word, such as happy, unhappy and happiness. Synonyms are words with similar meanings, antonyms are opposites.

points.ask: How do I make new words?

stages.title: Verb forms and time expressions
stages.hook: "I have lived here for five years" and "I lived here five years ago" - why are two tenses needed?
explain: English uses the present perfect (have/has plus past participle) to link past and present: "I have lived here for five years." Use the simple past for finished times: "I lived in Cairo in 2019."

Time words help. For and since go with the perfect: for five years, since 2020. Yesterday, last week and ago go with the simple past. Many irregular participles must be learned: written, spoken, taken, eaten.
stages.mnemonic: Since = starting point. For = how long.
items: from a point in the past until now
at some time up to now
sentences: We saw a film last night.

o: I have known her for ten years.
I know her for ten years.
I am knowing her since ten years.
I knew her since ten years.
gq.why: A situation that continues up to now takes the present perfect with for.

gq.q: Which time expression goes with the simple past?
gq.why: Yesterday names a finished time, so use the simple past.

panel.q: Why is "I have seen him yesterday" wrong?
o: Yesterday is a finished time, so the simple past is needed
Have cannot be used with seen
panel.why: The present perfect does not combine with a finished time word.

panel.q: Which is correct?
o: She has been here since Monday.
She has been here for Monday.
She is being here since Monday.
panel.why: Since is used with a starting point, and the present perfect is needed.

panel.q: Explain the difference between "I lost my keys" and "I have lost my keys".
panel.model: I lost my keys just reports a past event; I have lost my keys stresses that the result matters now - I still do not have them.
panel.why: Perfect highlights present relevance.

teach.model: The present perfect is have or has plus the past participle. It links past to now. Use for with a length of time and since with a starting point.

points.ask: Which time words go with it?

stages.title: Complex sentence introduction
stages.hook: How can you join "I was tired" and "I kept working" into one sentence?
explain: A complex sentence joins a main clause and a subordinate clause with a connector. Because, although, when, if and while are examples: "I kept working although I was tired."

The if-clause shows conditions: "If it rains, we will stay home." Relative clauses add information with who, which or that: "The girl who sits next to me is Aiko." Place a comma after an opening clause.
stages.mnemonic: Because gives the reason, although shows contrast, if sets the condition.
items: for a person in a relative clause
for a thing in a relative clause
sentences: If it rains, we will stay home.
I stayed home because I was ill.
The girl who sits here is Aiko.

o: If it rains, we will stay home.
If it will rain, we stay home.
If it rains, we stayed home.
If it rained, we will stay home.
gq.why: In a real future condition, if uses the present simple and the main clause uses will.

panel.q: Which is the correct relative pronoun? "The book ___ I bought is great."
panel.why: A thing is referred to by which or that.

panel.q: Why can we not say "Although he was tired, but he kept working"?
panel.model: Although and but both express contrast, so only one is used in English.
panel.why: Avoid doubling contrast words.

panel.q: Where does the comma go?
panel.why: A comma separates an opening subordinate clause from the main clause.

teach.model: You can join two ideas with a connector. Because gives a reason and although shows contrast. In if sentences, use the present simple after if and will in the main part.

points.ask: How do I give a reason?

stages.title: Reading short stories
stages.hook: A story begins: "The old lighthouse had been dark for years." What do you expect next?
explain: When we read a story, we look for characters, setting, problem and solution. We also infer: the story does not say everything, so we use clues. The words "had been dark for years" suggest the lighthouse was not used.
Titles, pictures and the first sentences help us predict. Look at the verb tenses: stories usually use the simple past, and the past perfect for events that happened earlier.
stages.mnemonic: Characters, setting, problem, solution: the story map.
items: where and when a story happens
a person who writes a story
sentences: The old lighthouse had been dark for years.

gq.q: What is the setting of a story?
"Tom had eaten before he arrived." Which happened first?
gq.why: The past perfect shows the earlier event.

panel.q: "Her smile faded as she read the letter." What can we infer?
o: The letter had bad or sad news
The letter made her very happy and excited
panel.why: A fading smile suggests a negative emotion; the text does not say so directly.

panel.q: Why do readers predict what will happen in a story?
panel.model: Predicting keeps you thinking about clues, which helps you understand and check your ideas as you read.
panel.why: Prediction supports comprehension.

panel.q: In "The wind howled," what is the howling?
o: Figurative language that gives the wind an animal sound
panel.why: Howling is a sound animals make, so the writer describes the wind in a figurative way that adds mood.

teach.topic: How to understand a short story
teach.model: Find the characters and the setting. Look for the problem and how it ends. Use clues in the text to guess things that are not written, which is called inferring.

points.ask: What do I look for first?
What happens in the middle and the end?
What if the story does not say it?

stages.title: Listening comprehension
stages.hook: On a station loudspeaker you hear: "The train to Leeds is delayed." What words do you catch first?
explain: Good listeners focus on key words, not every word. Content words (nouns, verbs, adjectives) get stress and are easier to hear. Little words like to, of and the are weak: "I want to go" sounds like "I wanna go" in fast speech.
Before you listen, think about the situation. Listen first for the main idea, then for details like numbers, times and names. It is normal to need to listen twice.
items: a place to wait for trains
to listen for the main idea
sentences: The train is delayed by ten minutes.
The next bus arrives at nine.

gq.q: In a fast sentence, which words are usually stressed?
o: Content words like nouns and verbs
gq.why: Stress falls on the meaningful words.

gq.q: What should you do first when you listen to a new recording?
gq.why: Listen for the gist first, then for details.

panel.q: "I'll see ya" - what is the full form?
panel.why: Fast speech reduces you to ya.

panel.q: Why is it hard to hear separate words in fast English?
panel.model: Words join together and small words are weak and short, so there are few gaps between them.
panel.why: Connected speech.

panel.q: Which numbers might be confused by listeners?
panel.why: Stress difference fif-TEEN versus FIF-ty.

teach.model: Do not try to catch every word. Listen for the gist first. Then listen again for details such as time, place and numbers.

points.ask: What do I listen for first?
What do I listen for second?

stages.title: Conversation and pronunciation
stages.hook: Why does "read" sound different in "I read every day" and "I read it yesterday"?
explain: Pronunciation covers sounds, stress and intonation. Intonation is the rise and fall of the voice. A question like "Are you coming?" usually rises at the end, but "Where are you going?" usually falls.

Some words have the same spelling but different pronunciations, like read /riːd/ and read /rɛd/. Others sound the same but are spelled differently: their and there, to, too and two. These are homophones.
stages.mnemonic: Voice up for yes/no, voice down for wh-.
items: a word that sounds like another
the rise and fall of the voice
a sound unit in a word
the strong beat of a word

gq.why: Their and there sound the same but have different meanings and spellings.

gq.q: How does the voice usually move at the end of "Are you ready?"
gq.why: Yes/no questions usually have rising intonation.

panel.q: Where is the stress in the noun "record" vs the verb "record"?
o: First syllable for the noun, second for the verb
Second syllable for the noun, first for the verb
panel.why: Some two-syllable words shift stress between noun and verb.

panel.q: Which word has a silent letter?
panel.why: The k in knee is not pronounced.

panel.q: How does stress change meaning in "I didn't say HE stole it" vs "I didn't SAY he stole it"?
panel.model: Stressing a different word focuses attention on a different part of the meaning.
panel.why: Sentence stress shows focus.

teach.model: Every word has a strong beat. A sentence also has a melody, called intonation. Your voice goes up for yes or no questions and down for wh- questions.

stages.title: Writing paragraphs
stages.hook: A good paragraph is like a sandwich. What are the layers?
explain: A paragraph has one main idea. Start with a topic sentence, add supporting details or examples, and end with a closing sentence. Linking words such as first, then, however and finally make the order clear.
Check your capital letters, full stops and spelling. Use new lines for new paragraphs. Read your writing aloud to hear mistakes.
stages.mnemonic: Topic sentence on top, details in the middle, closing at the bottom: a sandwich.
items: the sentence that gives the main idea
a fact that supports the idea
the last sentence of a paragraph

gq.q: What does a topic sentence do?
o: States the main idea of the paragraph

panel.q: Why should one paragraph hold only one main idea?
o: The reader can follow your thinking easily
It is a law of grammar
panel.why: A single focus makes the writing clear.

panel.q: How could you improve this: "I like dogs. Cats are cool. I went to the shop."?
panel.model: Choose one main idea, use a topic sentence, support it with details, and link the sentences.
panel.why: The sentences are unrelated.

panel.q: Which is the best closing sentence for a paragraph about a school garden?
o: In short, the garden teaches us to care for nature.
panel.why: A closing sentence sums up the main idea.

teach.model: Begin with a topic sentence that states your main idea. Add two or three details or examples. Finish with a closing sentence. Use words like first and finally to link ideas.

stages.title: Cultural expressions and idioms
stages.hook: If someone says "It's raining cats and dogs", should you look for animals?
explain: An idiom is a phrase whose meaning is not found in the separate words. "It's raining cats and dogs" means it is raining very hard. "Break a leg" means good luck, especially to performers. "Piece of cake" means very easy.
Idioms often depend on culture. In British English you might "have a cuppa", and an American may say "grab a coffee". Always check the meaning of an idiom in context before you use it.
stages.mnemonic: Do not translate word for word: picture the meaning, not the words.
items: to tell a secret by mistake
sentences: The test was a piece of cake.
I feel a bit under the weather.

gq.why: It is an idiom for feeling unwell.

gq.q: Your friend says "Break a leg!" before your concert. What does she mean?
gq.why: Break a leg is a traditional good-luck wish for performers.

panel.q: Why can idioms be hard for learners?
o: The meaning is not the sum of the words
panel.why: Idioms are fixed expressions with figurative meanings.

panel.q: What should you do if you hear an idiom you do not know?
panel.model: Use the context to guess, then ask or check a dictionary.
panel.why: Strategy for unknown idioms.

panel.q: Which is a British idiom for being very tired?
panel.why: Knackered is informal British English for exhausted.

teach.model: An idiom is a fixed phrase with a special meaning. Do not read it word by word. For example, a piece of cake means something is easy. Use the situation to understand it.

stages.title: Practical travel communication
stages.hook: You are lost at an airport. Which polite sentences will help you find your gate?
explain: Travel English uses polite requests: "Could you tell me where gate 12 is?" "How do I get to the city centre?" Use "Could" and "Would" for politeness. Use "I'd like to book a room" at a hotel.

Listen for numbers, times and directions: turn left, turn right, go straight on, next to, opposite. Signs often use short forms: Exit, Arrivals, Departures, Way out. British English uses lift where American English uses elevator, and train stations say platform in Britain and track in many US stations.
stages.mnemonic: Polite plus clear: Excuse me, could you...?
items: Could you tell me the way?
a paper to enter a plane
a document for travel to other countries
the place where bags come out
to ask politely where the toilet is
Could you tell me where the toilet is?
sentences: Could you tell me where gate twelve is?
I would like to book a room.

gq.q: Which is the most polite way to ask the way?
o: Excuse me, could you tell me how to get to the station?
gq.why: Excuse me and could you make a request polite.
Lift is British English; elevator is American.

panel.q: "Could you tell me where the bank is?" is correct. Which is also correct?
panel.why: Direct questions use inverted order; embedded questions use statement order.

panel.q: Why are indirect questions like "Could you tell me where the toilet is?" more polite than "Where is the toilet?"
panel.model: They sound softer because they ask for help rather than demanding information.
panel.why: Politeness in requests.

panel.q: A sign reads "Way out". What does it show?
panel.why: Way out is the British form of Exit.

teach.model: Use polite words to ask for help. Start with Excuse me and could you. Listen for directions like left, right and straight on, and check the numbers and times.
